html:
The Aghlabids were an Arab dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya, roughly modern Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya, from 800 to 909, nominally as governors for the Abbasid Caliphate. They are shown here in 800 and 900.

In 800 the caliph Harun al-Rashid made Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab hereditary governor in return for a yearly tribute. His descendants ran their own state from Kairouan and a palace city nearby. They rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan, built water reservoirs, and fortified the coast with ribats.

In 827 they began the conquest of Sicily, which took most of a century. They also took Malta in 870, and Muslim raiders from Africa and Sicily struck southern Italy and even attacked Rome in 846. The last Aghlabid fled in 909, when the Kutama Berbers led by an Ismaili missionary overthrew him and opened the way for the Fatimid Caliphate.
